sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** TLS (Transport Layer Security) is a cryptographic protocol layered between TCP and the application that authenticates one or both endpoints with X.509 certificates, negotiates symmetric session keys via an ephemeral key exchange, and then encrypts and integrity-protects every record flowing over the connection — SSL is the deprecated ancestor that gave the protocol family its popular name.
TLS is the trust backbone of the internet. Without it, every byte flowing over TCP — passwords, session cookies, API tokens, payment card numbers, video streams — would travel in cleartext, readable and mutable by any router, ISP, coffee-shop Wi-Fi, or compromised switch along the path. TLS solves three independent problems in one protocol: confidentiality (symmetric encryption prevents eavesdropping), integrity (AEAD tags prevent tampering), and authentication (X.509 certificates bind a server identity to a public key, validated through a chain rooted in a CA the client trusts). The handshake negotiates a cipher suite, authenticates the server (and optionally the client), derives shared symmetric keys via an ephemeral Diffie-Hellman exchange, and then both sides switch to encrypted records. Once the handshake completes, the cost is mostly the per-record AEAD computation, which modern CPUs handle at over 10 Gbps per core using AES-NI instructions.

The TLS 1.3 handshake (RFC 8446, 2018) is a major redesign over TLS 1.2. The client sends ClientHello containing supported cipher suites, the SNI (Server Name Indication), and crucially a Diffie-Hellman key_share — the client's ephemeral public value. The server replies in the same flight with ServerHello (its chosen cipher and DH share), Certificate, CertVerify (a signature over the handshake transcript proving possession of the private key), and Finished (a MAC over the transcript). At this point both sides have enough material to derive the shared secret via ECDHE, so the client sends Finished and immediately starts sending encrypted application data. This collapses the handshake to 1 RTT instead of TLS 1.2's 2 RTT — a 200 ms saving on a typical mobile network. TLS 1.3 also supports 0-RTT for resumed sessions: a returning client uses a pre-shared key (PSK) derived from the previous session's resumption secret to encrypt early data on its very first flight. 0-RTT is great for latency-sensitive apps but has a replay risk, so it must never be used for non-idempotent requests like POST /checkout.

TLS 1.3 also removed all the weak primitives that haunted earlier versions. RSA key transport (where the client encrypted the session key under the server's RSA public key) is gone — every cipher suite now uses ephemeral Diffie-Hellman, which means perfect forward secrecy is mandatory. An attacker who records all your traffic today and steals the server's private key tomorrow still cannot decrypt the recorded traffic, because the per-session DH secrets were ephemeral and discarded at connection close. Static Diffie-Hellman, CBC-mode ciphers, SHA-1, MD5, and RC4 are all removed. The remaining cipher suites are tiny and modern: `TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256`, `TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384`, `TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256`, and `TLS_AES_128_CCM_SHA256`. ChaCha20-Poly1305 is favored on mobile devices without AES-NI (older ARM chips) because it is constant-time in software and faster than AES-GCM there.

Real systems depend on TLS at every layer. Cloudflare terminates TLS for over 30 million internet properties for free, using a globally distributed key server and keyless SSL so that private keys never leave the customer's hardware. Netflix encrypts its video streams with TLS end-to-end between Open Connect appliances and player clients, both to protect content licensing and to prevent ISP injection of ads or throttling markers. Inside the datacenter, service meshes like Istio and Linkerd use mutual TLS (mTLS) for every service-to-service call, rotating client certs every 24 hours via SPIFFE/SPIRE so that a compromised pod cannot impersonate another service for long. Google's internal LoAS/ALTS system does the same at planet scale. Certificate issuance used to be a manual pain point, but Let's Encrypt's free ACME-automated certificates and AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) have made auto-renewing TLS the default rather than the exception.

The biggest operational pitfall is certificate revocation. When a private key is compromised or a cert is misissued, the CA publishes a revocation — but clients historically did not reliably check CRLs (Certificate Revocation Lists) because the download was large and slow. OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol) was introduced to query revocation status per cert, but it leaked browsing history to the CA and added latency. OCSP stapling solves both: the server fetches a signed OCSP response from the CA every few hours and "staples" it to its TLS handshake, so the client gets revocation status without an extra round trip and without leaking to the CA. Must-staple certs (with the `tlsfeature` extension) refuse to validate if a stapled response is missing. Another pitfall is mismatched cipher suite support between client and server — old Android clients may not have ChaCha20, while modern servers disable CBC-mode ciphers, leading to handshake failures that are hard to debug without a tool like `openssl s_client`. TLS also adds CPU cost and handshake latency, which is why connection reuse (HTTP keep-alive, HTTP/2 multiplexing, connection pooling) is so important for high-throughput systems.

TLS connects deeply to other system design concepts. It is the substrate that makes HTTPS (Phase 2 Topic 4) trustworthy, and it is the transport for HTTP/2 and HTTP/3. The 1-RTT vs 2-RTT handshake decision feeds directly into the cold-connection latency budget we discussed in Phase 1 Topic 8. mTLS in service meshes is the foundation of zero-trust networking, replacing network-level trust (VPC peering) with cryptographically verifiable workload identity. The certificate authority hierarchy is itself a study in distributed trust — a single CA compromise (like DigiNotar in 2011) can compromise millions of sites, which is why browsers now require CT (Certificate Transparency) logs that publicly record every issued cert so misissuance is detectable. Understanding TLS deeply is essential because every API call, every database connection over TLS (like Postgres `sslmode=verify-full`), and every service mesh handshake depends on it.

sections.body:
### Mermaid Diagram ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant C as Client participant S as Server participant CA as Certificate Authority Note over C,S: TLS 1.3 Handshake (1 RTT) C->>S: ClientHello (version, ciphers, SNI, key_share, PSK?) S->>C: ServerHello (chosen cipher, key_share) S->>C: Certificate (chain) + CertVerify + Finished Note over C: Verify chain to trusted root
Check hostname in SAN
Check OCSP staple C->>S: Finished + app data (encrypted) Note over C,S: Application data flows both ways under AEAD C->>S: GET /api/users (encrypted record) S->>C: 200 OK + JSON body (encrypted record) Note over C,CA: Optional: OCSP request for revocation status
(or via stapled response) ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` +-----------+ ClientHello +-----------+ | Client | --------------------------> | Server | | (browser) | version, ciphers, SNI, | (nginx) | +-----------+ key_share(ECDHE_pub_C) +-----------+ ^ | | | Server picks cipher + ECDHE_priv_S | | Looks up cert chain for SNI | v +-----------+ ServerHello + Certificate +-----------+ | Client | <-------------------------- | Server | | verifies | key_share(ECDHE_pub_S), | signs | | cert | CertVerify(sig), Finished | transcript| | chain | | with priv | +-----------+ +-----------+ | | derives shared_secret = ECDHE(C_priv, S_pub) | == ECDHE(S_priv, C_pub) on server side v +-----------+ Finished + app data +-----------+ | Client | --------------------------> | Server | | sends | (all encrypted AEAD) | derives | | GET /api | | same key | +-----------+ +-----------+ | v +-----------------+ | Application | | data flows | | AES-128-GCM or | | ChaCha20-P1305 | +-----------------+ Certificate chain: leaf (api.example.com) <-- signed by -- | | v | intermediate (Let's Encrypt R3) <------ | | v | root (ISRG Root X1) <-- in client trust store ``` ### Walkthrough 1. Client opens a TCP connection and sends ClientHello listing supported TLS versions, cipher suites, the SNI (`api.example.com`), and an ephemeral ECDHE public key share. 2. Server selects the strongest mutually supported cipher suite (e.g., `TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256`), generates its own ephemeral ECDHE key pair, and replies with ServerHello + Certificate (leaf + intermediate) + CertVerify (signature over the transcript using the cert's private key) + Finished (MAC over the transcript). 3. Client verifies the cert chain reaches a trusted root, checks the hostname matches a SAN entry, checks the OCSP staple for revocation status, then derives the shared secret via ECDHE. It sends Finished and immediately starts sending encrypted application data. 4. Server derives the same shared secret, verifies the client's Finished MAC, and starts sending encrypted responses. Both sides now exchange AEAD-protected records using AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305 until the connection is closed with a `close_notify` alert.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- TLS 1.3 handshake state-machine simulator (educational, no real crypto).
- Demonstrates the message flow, cert chain verification, and state transitions.
- Server flight: ServerHello + Certificate + CertVerify + Finished (+ OCSP staple)
- Accept 0-RTT only if PSK matches and the early data looks idempotent
- 1. Verify cert chain reaches a trusted root
- 2. Verify hostname in leaf SAN
- 3. Check OCSP staple
- 4. Verify CertVerify signature (placeholder: assume valid)

**Defines:** `State`, `HandshakeMessage`, `Cert`, `TLSEndpoint`, `run_tls_1_3_handshake()`

```python
# TLS 1.3 handshake state-machine simulator (educational, no real crypto).
# Demonstrates the message flow, cert chain verification, and state transitions.

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from enum import Enum, auto
from typing import Optional

class State(Enum):
    START = auto()
    CLIENT_HELLO_SENT = auto()
    SERVER_HELLO_SENT = auto()
    CLIENT_FINISHED_SENT = auto()
    CONNECTED = auto()
    CLOSED = auto()

@dataclass
class HandshakeMessage:
    name: str
    payload: dict

@dataclass
class Cert:
    cn: str
    san: list
    issuer: str
    valid_until: str
    serial: str
    must_staple: bool = False

@dataclass
class TLSEndpoint:
    role: str                          # "client" or "server"
    state: State = State.START
    sent: list = field(default_factory=list)
    received: list = field(default_factory=list)
    cipher: Optional[str] = None
    shared_secret: Optional[bytes] = None
    cert_chain: list = field(default_factory=list)
    psk: Optional[bytes] = None        # resumption pre-shared key
    early_data_sent: bool = False

    # ---------- Client ----------
    def send_client_hello(self, sni: str, offer_0rtt: bool = False) -> HandshakeMessage:
        assert self.role == "client" and self.state == State.START
        payload = {
            "versions": ["tls1.3"],
            "ciphers": ["TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256", "TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256"],
            "key_share_c": b"ecdhe_pub_client_abc",
            "sni": sni,
            "random": b"client_random_xxxxxx",
        }
        if offer_0rtt and self.psk:
            payload["psk"] = self.psk
            payload["early_data"] = b"GET /home HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: " + sni.encode() + b"\r\n\r\n"
            self.early_data_sent = True
        msg = HandshakeMessage("ClientHello", payload)
        self.sent.append(msg)
        self.state = State.CLIENT_HELLO_SENT
        return msg

    # ---------- Server ----------
    def handle_client_hello(self, msg: HandshakeMessage, cert_chain: list,
                            trusted_roots: set, ocsp_status: str = "good") -> list:
        assert self.role == "server" and self.state == State.START
        self.received.append(msg)
        self.cipher = "TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256"        # pick strongest
        self.cert_chain = cert_chain
        # Server flight: ServerHello + Certificate + CertVerify + Finished (+ OCSP staple)
        flight = [
            HandshakeMessage("ServerHello", {
                "version": "tls1.3",
                "cipher": self.cipher,
                "key_share_s": b"ecdhe_pub_server_xyz",
                "random": b"server_random_yyyyyy",
            }),
            HandshakeMessage("Certificate", {"chain": cert_chain}),
            HandshakeMessage("CertVerify", {"sig": b"ecdsa_sig_over_transcript"}),
            HandshakeMessage("Finished", {"verify_data": b"server_finished_mac"}),
            HandshakeMessage("OCSPStaple", {"status": ocsp_status, "valid_until": "2025-01-15"}),
        ]
        # Accept 0-RTT only if PSK matches and the early data looks idempotent
        if msg.payload.get("psk") == self.psk and msg.payload.get("early_data"):
            flight.append(HandshakeMessage("EncryptedExtensions", {"0rtt_accepted": True}))
        self.sent.extend(flight)
        self.state = State.SERVER_HELLO_SENT
        return flight

    # ---------- Client ----------
    def handle_server_flight(self, flight: list, trusted_roots: set,
                             expected_hostname: str) -> None:
        assert self.role == "client" and self.state == State.CLIENT_HELLO_SENT
        self.received.extend(flight)
        # 1. Verify cert chain reaches a trusted root
        cert_msg = next(m for m in flight if m.name == "Certificate")
        chain = cert_msg.payload["chain"]
        if chain[-1].issuer not in trusted_roots and chain[-1].cn not in trusted_roots:
            raise ValueError(f"chain does not reach a trusted root: ends at {chain[-1].cn}")
        # 2. Verify hostname in leaf SAN
        leaf = chain[0]
        if expected_hostname not in leaf.san:
            raise ValueError(f"hostname mismatch: {expected_hostname} not in {leaf.san}")
        # 3. Check OCSP staple
        ocsp = next(m for m in flight if m.name == "OCSPStaple")
        if ocsp.payload["status"] != "good":
            raise ValueError(f"cert revoked: {ocsp.payload['status']}")
        if leaf.must_staple and ocsp is None:
            raise ValueError("must-staple cert but no OCSP staple present")
        # 4. Verify CertVerify signature (placeholder: assume valid)
        # 5. Derive shared secret via ECDHE (placeholder bytes)
        self.shared_secret = b"derived_session_key_zzz"
        self.cipher = "TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256"
        self.sent.append(HandshakeMessage("Finished", {"verify_data": b"client_finished_mac"}))
        self.state = State.CLIENT_FINISHED_SENT

    # ---------- Server ----------
    def handle_client_finished(self, msg: HandshakeMessage) -> None:
        assert self.role == "server" and self.state == State.SERVER_HELLO_SENT
        self.received.append(msg)
        self.shared_secret = b"derived_session_key_zzz"
        self.state = State.CONNECTED

    def finalize(self) -> None:
        if self.role == "client":
            assert self.state == State.CLIENT_FINISHED_SENT
        self.state = State.CONNECTED

    def send_app_data(self, data: bytes) -> None:
        assert self.state == State.CONNECTED, "must finish handshake first"
        tag = b"aead_tag_xx"                      # placeholder for AES-GCM tag
        print(f"  [{self.role}] >> {len(data)}B encrypted record, cipher={self.cipher}, tag={tag.hex()}")

def run_tls_1_3_handshake():
    print("=== TLS 1.3 Handshake Simulator ===\n")
    # Cert chain: leaf -> intermediate -> root
    root = Cert(cn="ISRG Root X1", san=[], issuer="ISRG Root X1", valid_until="2035-06-04", serial="r001")
    intermediate = Cert(cn="Let's Encrypt R3", san=[], issuer="ISRG Root X1", valid_until="2025-09-15", serial="i0042")
    leaf = Cert(cn="api.example.com", san=["api.example.com", "example.com"],
                issuer="Let's Encrypt R3", valid_until="2025-03-01", serial="l99213", must_staple=True)
    chain = [leaf, intermediate, root]
    trusted_roots = {"ISRG Root X1"}

    client = TLSEndpoint(role="client")
    server = TLSEndpoint(role="server")

    # Step 1: ClientHello (1st flight from client)
    ch = client.send_client_hello(sni="api.example.com", offer_0rtt=False)
    print(f"1. client -> server : {ch.name}")
    print(f"   sni={ch.payload['sni']}, ciphers={ch.payload['ciphers']}")
    print(f"   key_share_c={ch.payload['key_share_c'][:10]}... (ephemeral ECDHE pub)")

    # Step 2: Server flight
    flight = server.handle_client_hello(ch, chain, trusted_roots, ocsp_status="good")
    print(f"\n2. server -> client : {[m.name for m in flight]}")
    print(f"   chosen cipher: {server.cipher}")

    # Step 3: Client verifies cert chain, sends Finished
    client.handle_server_flight(flight, trusted_roots, expected_hostname="api.example.com")
    print(f"\n3. client -> server : Finished")
    print(f"   cert chain verified to root: {chain[-1].cn}")
    print(f"   leaf SAN check OK, OCSP status: good, must_staple satisfied")

    # Step 4: Server receives Finished, both CONNECTED
    server.handle_client_finished(client.sent[-1])
    client.finalize()
    print(f"\n4. both endpoints: state={client.state.name}, shared_secret_match={client.shared_secret == server.shared_secret}")

    # Application data over encrypted channel
    print("\n=== Application Data (AEAD-encrypted records) ===")
    client.send_app_data(b"GET /api/users HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: api.example.com\r\n\r\n")
    server.send_app_data(b"HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Type: application/json\r\n\r\n[{\"id\":1}]")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    run_tls_1_3_handshake()
```

SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) is the original protocol developed by Netscape in the mid-1990s; versions SSL 2.0 (1995) and SSL 3.0 (1996) had serious cryptographic flaws…
quiz.explanation: SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) is the original protocol developed by Netscape in the mid-1990s; versions SSL 2.0 (1995) and SSL 3.0 (1996) had serious cryptographic flaws (weak MAC-then-encrypt, no PFS, BEAST/POODLE attacks). The IETF took over the protocol and renamed it TLS starting with TLS 1.0 (1999), which was essentially SSL 3.1.

quiz.explanation: Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS) means that even if the server's long-term private key is leaked in the future, all past recorded traffic remains confidential. This is achieved by using ephemeral Diffie-Hellman (ECDHE) for every session's key exchange: each connection derives its symmetric keys from random per-session DH values that are erased when the connection closes.
